en: The Sūtra of the Simile of the Five Aggregates, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the country of Mi-sheng; crossing a river ferry, he saw a large crowd.
A mass of foam drifting with the current, he then addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "Bhikṣus!

Just as this great mass of foam drifts with the current, a person with sight who sees it, observes it, and examines it, immediately knows it to be non-existent, empty, unreal, quickly dissolving, and destined for extinction."
Why is that? Because foam has no substance.
Thus it is, bhikṣus!

Regarding all forms—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; coarse or subtle; beautiful or ugly; distant or near—a bhikṣu should examine them with thorough scrutiny and contemplation. He should see that they do not exist, being empty, non-substantial, merely a disease, merely a knot, merely a boil, and merely a deception; they are not real, not permanent, suffering, empty, non-self, and subject to exhaustion.
Why is this? Because the nature of form has no strength.
For example, O bhikṣu!

When the heavens rain down drops of water, each bubble as it arises immediately perishes; a person with sight who observes, contemplates, and examines them knows at once that they are not real, empty, unsubstantial, quickly vanishing, and destined for extinction.
Why is that? Because a bubble has no strength.
Thus it is, bhikṣus!

Regarding all that is painful—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; coarse or subtle; beautiful or ugly; far or near—a bhikṣu should see and know it, and examine it thoroughly. He should contemplate it as non-existent, empty, unreal, being merely a disease, merely a knot, merely a deception, and merely a sore; it is not true, it is impermanent, it is suffering, it is empty, it is non-self, and it is subject to exhaustion.
Why is this? Because the nature of sensation has no strength.
"For example, bhikṣus!..."

In the intense heat of midsummer, when the sun blazes at its zenith, a person with sight observes, contemplates, and examines it; they immediately know it is not real, empty, unsubstantial, quickly vanishing, and destined for extinction.
Why is that? Because the mirage has no substance.
Thus it is, bhikṣus!

Regarding all perceptions—past, future, and present; internal and external; coarse and subtle; beautiful and ugly; far and near—a bhikṣu should examine them thoroughly, scrutinize them, and contemplate them: that they do not exist, being empty, unreal, merely lust, merely fetters, merely sores, and merely deceptions; that they are not true, not permanent, suffering, empty, non-self, and subject to exhaustion.
Why is this so? Because the nature of perception has no strength.
"For example, bhikṣus!..."

Suppose a person seeking fine timber takes up an axe and enters a forest; there he sees a large plantain tree, tall and straight without any curvature. He cuts its base, hacks its top, and splits its leaves; as he peels it layer by layer until it is completely resolved, he finds that in its very core there is no heartwood—how could there be any solidity?
When a person of insight sees it, observes it, and examines it, they immediately know it to be non-existent, empty, unreal, swiftly vanishing, and destined for extinction. Why is this so?
Because that plantain tree has no strength;

even so, bhikṣu! Regarding all conditioned phenomena—past, future, and present; internal or external; coarse or fine; beautiful or ugly; far or near—a bhikṣu should see them and examine them thoroughly, knowing that they do not exist, being empty, unreal, merely lust, merely fetters, merely sores, merely deceptions, non-self, impermanent, suffering, empty, non-substantial, and subject to exhaustion.
Why is this? Because the nature of practice has no rigidity.
"For example, bhikṣu!..."
A magician and his apprentice, amidst a great multitude at a crossroads, manifested various illusions, conjuring herds of elephants, troops of horses, chariots, and infantry.

When the man with eyes sees it, observes it, and examines it, he immediately knows that it does not exist, is empty and void, unreal, formless, a transformation, and subject to exhaustion. Why is this so?
Because an illusion has no strength. Thus it is, bhikṣu!

All that is cognized—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; coarse or subtle; beautiful or ugly; far or near—a bhikṣu should see these things and examine them thoroughly. He should observe that they do not exist, being empty, unreal, merely lust, merely fetters, merely sores, merely deceptions; they are not true, not permanent, suffering, empty, non-self, and subject to exhaustion.
"Why is this? Because the nature of consciousness has no strength.
Thereupon, the Buddha spoke these verses:
"Form is likened to a mass of foam, Sensation is like a bubble on the water,
Perception is compared to a mirage in the heat, Volitional formations are like the trunk of a plantain tree,
And consciousness is illustrated by a magical illusion— Thus have the Buddhas taught."
One should regard this as the essential contemplation; examine it thoroughly and reflect upon it.
To discern the nature of emptiness and find no permanence therein—this is how one should view the aggregates (*skandhas*); such is what true wisdom teaches.
When these three things are severed, one knows that the body has no value;
life-force, warmth, and consciousness depart from the body and pass away.
As it lies dead upon the ground, it is like grass, devoid of all sensation.
Observing its nature to be thus, it is merely an illusion yet people are deluded and greedy.
Mind after mind finds no peace, nor is there any stability;
knowing the five aggregates to be like this, a bhikṣu should apply himself with diligent effort.
"Therefore, throughout day and night, one should personally awaken to mindfulness and right knowledge;
practicing the path of tranquility, the practice of relinquishment brings the highest peace.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they were all filled with joy.
*The Sūtra of the Simile of the Five Aggregates*.
